title: Babylon falls (Apocalypse 18)
hookLine: the merchants weep over a city built on luxury

lines: THE SAME LIST, IN THE APOCALYPSE.
cards: Open a shopping app and scroll. Gold jewelry. Silk scarves.
Everything delivered to your door, from somewhere you'll never see, made by people you'll never meet.
Now read chapter eighteen of the Apocalypse, and you'll find almost the same list: gold, silver, pearls, silk, scarlet, ivory, cinnamon, perfume, wine, oil, fine flour, cattle, horses, chariots.

teach.h: BABYLON: A CODE NAME FOR ROME.
teach.b: In the Apocalypse, Babylon is a code name, and a long line of readers have taken it as Rome: chapter seventeen speaks of seven mountains, and Rome was rich, powerful, and hard on those who wouldn't bow.
The first letter of Peter seems to use the same code, sending greetings from the church in Babylon.
In chapter eighteen an angel lights up the earth with his glory and cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen."

teach.h: GO OUT FROM HER, MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: Then a voice from heaven: "Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins."
Then three groups of mourners: kings who lived in luxury with her, merchants who got rich off her, sailors who carried her cargo.
They stand far off, afraid, saying the same thing: in one hour her judgment came; in one hour her riches were laid waste. Three times the text says it. Listen to the list to the very end.

teach.h: THE LIST ENDS WITH HUMAN SOULS.
teach.b: After the horses and chariots, the last items are bodies and human souls. People, bought and sold like the cinnamon. That's what the luxury was standing on.
Then an angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea: like that, Babylon will be thrown down and found no more. No more music in her streets, no more lamps, no more bride and bridegroom.
The chapter isn't against beauty or trade. It's about a whole way of life that forgot people were not merchandise, and how fast it can vanish. Catholic social teaching makes a similar warning.

how: Catholic social teaching warns against consumerism and insists that people are never merchandise; Catholics practice simplicity through fasting and almsgiving, especially in Lent, and support fair labor and the fight against human trafficking.

o: a proud city of luxury, built on traded lives, gone in an hour
a tower whose builders were scattered into many tongues
the old city on the Euphrates, conquered by Persia

p: a code name, read as Rome

s: in the Apocalypse, Babylon simply means the old city on the Euphrates
it's a code name, and a long line of readers have taken it as Rome.
the merchants' cargo list ends with human beings
after horses and chariots: bodies and human souls.
the mourners say 'in one hour' three times
in one hour her judgment came, her riches laid waste.

games.q: you live in the great city. the voice from heaven says something about your life there. what does it say?
o: stay and enjoy it while it lasts.
go out from her, my people, so you don't share in her sins.
buy what you can before the fall.
games.why: go out from her, my people. not a call to leave a map location, some readers say, but to stop living by the city's values.

practice: Bring to mind the last few things you bought or almost bought, and pick one you didn't really need, the one that was more about the scroll than the need; imagine not buying it, and notice if anything in you protests.
Then think about who made the things you do buy: the hands, the fields, the factories, the drivers. If you pray, pray for them; if not, just hold them in mind for a moment, people, not merchandise.

wordCard.voice: Babylon falls. Apocalypse eighteen: the great city of luxury, built on bought and sold lives, laid waste in one hour. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great (Apocalypse 18:2), echoing Isaiah 21:9.

carryVoice: Your line: what doesn't last. In one hour, all of it was gone. That's six hundred twenty-eight days.
